headline: Anthropic's IPO: Genius Machines, Collapsing Humans, No Problem
subheadline: Wall Street celebrates AI's brightest hour while its makers navigate scandal, financial chaos, and open revolt.
source_headline: AI's great divergence: Machines accelerate as makers unravel
body_html:
Anthropic makes its Wall Street debut this week in what can only be described as the most honest mirror ever held up to venture capital: a company built on superintelligence going public at the precise moment its entire species—the humans running it—is bogged down by scandal, financial turmoil, and what Axios delicately calls "political revolt." The timing is not incidental. It is the entire business model made visible. The machines are ascending while the makers are collapsing, and investors have decided this is exactly when to pay the most.

For those unfamiliar, Anthropic is an AI safety company that makes Claude, a large language model positioned as the responsible, constitutional answer to ChatGPT's chaos. The company was founded by defectors from OpenAI who believed they could build artificial intelligence the right way—with safety, alignment, ethics, and restraint built in from the start. It is a noble mission. It is also currently losing a custody battle with its own founders, who apparently have discovered that being the architect of artificial superintelligence is less rewarding than the scandal and turmoil that comes with actually trying to sell it.

The historical precedent here is thin, which is precisely what makes it valuable. We have watched OpenAI tear itself apart over governance. We have watched Meta spend billions on a metaverse that nobody wanted. We have watched crypto collapse under the weight of its own visionary certitude. What we have not often witnessed is a company going public while its leadership structure is actively malfunctioning—and the market enthusiastically rewarding it anyway. Anthropic's debut is the logical endpoint of a decade of venture capital learning that dysfunction at the top is merely "story" and story is valuable.

The pitch, naturally, is that the technology is so revolutionary, so existentially important, that the minor matter of human governance becomes almost quaint. The machines are "accelerating toward an intelligence explosion," per company framing. Translation: we have built something we don't entirely understand and cannot fully control, and that is expensive. Translation of the translation: please pay now.

What could go wrong? Everything. The AI arms race rewards speed over stability. The moment Anthropic's safety-first ethos conflicts with margin pressure or market competition, we will learn whether "constitutional AI" is an operating principle or a marketing tagline. The humans running the company are already in open conflict. When—not if—the first major alignment failure or misuse incident occurs, those same fractured leaders will be expected to manage a public crisis while their own governance implodes live on CNBC.

This deal is a perfect encapsulation of 2024 venture capital: infinite faith in the machines, zero faith in the people building them, and the absolute certainty that this contradiction will somehow resolve in everyone's favor. The IPO is not despite the dysfunction. It is because of it. A smoothly run company with stable leadership would raise boring questions about valuation. A company in chaos, led by brilliant people tearing each other apart, raising the stakes to civilization-level proportions? That's a story worth billions.

The machines are probably fine. The humans definitely are not. And Wall Street could not be more excited about it.
glossary_definition: A framework for training artificial intelligence with safety guardrails, until market pressure and competitive necessity make those guardrails optionally performative.
